items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.

items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.

items.title: Harold won the first battle of 1066 — then lost the second three weeks later
items.claim: King Harold Godwinson fought two major battles in 1066. What happened?

options.text: Hastings was his only battle of the year
He defeated Harald Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then marched 250 miles south and lost to William at Hastings on 14 October
He won at Hastings but died of wounds soon after
He defeated William at Hastings, then was killed by Harald Hardrada

items.reveal:
Harald Hardrada of Norway and Harold's exiled brother Tostig landed in Yorkshire in September 1066. Harold marched north and crushed them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September — Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

Three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey. Harold's exhausted army marched south and met William at Senlac Hill near Hastings on 14 October. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Harold's death; the Bayeux Tapestry depicts a figure with an arrow to the eye, though the identification is debated.
items.why: The Conquest is taught as a single event. It was actually a year of crisis with two invasions, one of which Harold won. Without Stamford Bridge weakening his army, Hastings might have gone the other way.
